L16@P0: Funding: This work was partly funded by DFG Grant 389792660 as part of TRR 248 (Foundations of Perspicuous Software Systems), the Cluster of Excellence EXC 2050/1 (CeTI, project ID 390696704, as part of Germany’s
L17@P0: Excellence Strategy), and the DFG projects BA-1679/11-1 and BA-1679/12-1.
L18@P0: Investigations of causality in operational systems aim at providing human-understandable explanations of why a system behaves as it does. There is, in particular, a demand to explain what went wrong
L19@P0: on a given counterexample execution that shows that a system does not satisfy a given specification.
L20@P0: To this end, this paper investigates a notion of counterfactual causality in transition systems based
L21@P0: on Stalnaker’s and Lewis’ semantics of counterfactuals in terms of most similar possible worlds
L22@P0: and introduces a novel corresponding notion of counterfactual causality in two-player games. Using
L23@P0: distance functions between paths in transition systems to capture the similarity of executions, this
L24@P0: notion defines whether reaching a certain set of states is a cause for the fact that a given execution of
L25@P0: a system satisfies an undesirable reachability or safety property. Similarly, using distance functions
L26@P0: between memoryless strategies in reachability and safety games, it is defined whether reaching a set
L27@P0: of states is a cause for the fact that a given strategy for the player under investigation is losing.
L28@P0: The contribution of the paper is two-fold: In transition systems, it is shown that counterfactual
L29@P0: causality can be checked in polynomial time for three prominent distance functions between paths.
L30@P0: In two-player games, the introduced notion of counterfactual causality is shown to be checkable in
L31@P0: polynomial time for two natural distance functions between memoryless strategies. Further, a notion
L32@P0: of explanation that can be extracted from a counterfactual cause and that pinpoints changes to be
L33@P0: made to the given strategy in order to transform it into a winning strategy is defined. For the two
L34@P0: distance functions under consideration, the problem to decide whether such an explanation imposes
L35@P0: only minimal necessary changes to the given strategy with respect to the used distance function
L36@P0: turns out to be coNP-complete and not to be solvable in polynomial time if P is not equal to NP,
L37@P0: respectively.
L38@P0: 1 Introduction
L39@P0: Modern software and hardware systems have reached a level of complexity that makes it impossible for
L40@P0: humans to assess whether a system behaves as intended without tools tailored for this task. To tackle this
L41@P0: problem, automated verification techniques have been developed. Model checking is one prominent such
L42@P0: technique: A model-checking algorithm takes a mathematical model of the system under investigation
L43@P0-1: arXiv:2308.11385v1 [cs.LO] 22 Aug 20232 Counterfactual Causality for Reachability and Safety
L44@P1: and a formal specification of the intended behavior and determines whether all possible executions of the
L45@P1: model satisfy the specification. While the results of a model-checking algorithm provide guarantees on
L46@P1: the correctness of a system or affirm the presence of an error, their usefulness is, nevertheless, limited as
L47@P1: they do not provide a human-understandable explanation of the behavior of the system.
L48@P1: To provide additional information on why the system behaves as it does, certificates witnessing the
L49@P1: result of the model-checking procedure, in particular counterexample traces in case of a negative result,
L50@P1: have been studied extensively (see, e.g., [9, 29, 10, 30]). Due to the potentially still enormous size of
L51@P1: counterexample traces and other certificates, a line of research has emerged that tries to distill comprehensible explications of what causes the system to behave as it does using formalizations of causality
L52@P1: (see, e.g., [31, 32, 2]).
L53@P1: Forward- and backward-looking causality There are two fundamentally different types of notions
L54@P1: of causality: forward-looking and backward-looking notions [37]. In the context of operational system
L55@P1: models, forward-looking causality describes general causal relations between events that might happen
L56@P1: along some possible executions. Backward-looking causality, on the other hand, addresses the causal
L57@P1: relation between events along a given execution of the system model. This distinction is captured in more
L58@P1: general contexts by the distinction between type-level causality addressing general causal dependencies
L59@P1: between events that might happen when looking forward in a world model, and token-level or actual
L60@P1: causality, corresponding to the backward view, that addresses causes for a particular event that actually
L61@P1: happened (see, e.g., [16]).
L62@P1: Notions of necessary causality are typically forward-looking: A necessary cause C for an effect E is
L63@P1: an event that occurs on every execution that exhibits the effect E (see, e.g., [3], and for a philosophical
L64@P1: analysis of necessity in causes [28]). The backward view naturally arises when the task is to explain what
L65@P1: went wrong after an undesired effect has been observed. In the verification context, the backward view is
L66@P1: natural for explaining counterexamples, see e.g. [42, 6, 15, 33, 38, 39]. Most of these techniques rely on
L67@P1: the counterfactuality principle, which has been originally studied in philosophy [20, 21, 36, 26, 27] and
L68@P1: formalized mathematically by Halpern and Pearl [17, 18, 19, 16]. Intuitively, counterfactual causality
L69@P1: requires that the effect would not have happened, if the cause had not occurred, in combination with
L70@P1: some minimality constraints for causes. The most prominent account for the semantics of the involved
L71@P1: counterfactual implication is provided by Stalnaker and Lewis [36, 26, 27] in terms of closest, i.e., most
L72@P1: similar, possible worlds. The statement “if the cause C had not occurred, then the effect E would not
L73@P1: have occurred” holds true if in the worlds that are most similar to the actual world and in which C did
L74@P1: not occur, E also did not occur. Interpreting executions of a system as possible worlds, the actual world
L75@P1: is an execution π where both the effect E and its counterfactual cause C occur, while the effect E does
L76@P1: not occur in alternative executions that are as similar as possible to π and that do not exhibit C.
L77@P1: For a more detailed discussion on the distinction between forward- and backward looking causality
L78@P1: and related concepts for responsibility, we refer the reader, e.g., to [37, 40, 41, 4, 2].
L79@P1: Defining counterfactual causality in transition systems and reachability games To define our backwardlooking notion of counterfactual causality in transition systems, we follow an approach similar to the one
L80@P1: by Groce et al [14] who presented a Stalnaker-Lewis-style formalization of counterfactual dependence of
L81@P1: events using distance functions. We consider the case where effects are reachability or safety properties
L82@P1: and causes are sets of states. To illustrate the idea, let T be a transition system and let E and C be disjoint sets of states of T indicating a reachability effect and a potential cause, respectively. Consider an

L177@P3: Contributions
L178@P3: • We show that d-counterfactual causal relationships in transition systems (defined as in [14]) can
L179@P3: be checked in polynomial time for the following three distance metrics d (Sec. 3.2):
L180@P3: 1. the prefix distance: paths are more similar if their traces share a longer prefix.
L181@P3: 2. the Hamming distance that counts the positions at which traces of paths differ.
L182@P3: 3. the Levenshtein distance that counts how many insertions, deletions, and substitutions are
L183@P3: necessary to transform the trace of one path to the trace of another path.
L184@P3: Furthermore, we show that the notion of d-counterfactual causality for the Hamming distance is
L185@P3: consistent with Halpern and Pearl’s but-for causes [18, 19].
L186@P3: • In reachability games, we provide a generalization of this notion using similarity metrics on memoryless deterministic strategies. We show that for the Hausdorff lifting of the prefix distance on
L187@P3: paths to a distance function on memoryless deterministic strategies, the resulting notion can be
L188@P3: checked in polynomial time (Sec. 4.1).
L189@P3: • We introduce a notion of counterfactual explanation that can be computed from a counterfactual
L190@P3: cause (Sec. 4.2). An explanation specifies where a non-winning strategy needs to be changed. Of
L191@P3: particular interest are D-minimal explanations that enforce only minimal necessary changes with
L192@P3: respect to a distance function D on strategies. For two distance functions related to the Hamming
L193@P3: distance, we show that checking whether an explanation is minimal is coNP-complete and not in
L194@P3: P if P̸=NP, respectively.
L195@P3: An overview of the complexity results can be found in Table 1.
L196@P3: Related work Ways to pinpoint the problematic steps in a counterexample trace by localizing errors
L197@P3: have widely been studied [42, 6, 15, 33, 38, 39]. For counterfactuality in transition systems, we follow
L198@P3-4: the approach of [14] with distance metrics. In contrast to the causes in this paper, causes in [14] areJ. Parreaux, J. Piribauer, and C. Baier 5
L199@P4: formulas in an expressive logic that can precisely talk about the valuation of variables after a certain
L200@P4: number of steps. Further [14] is not concerned with checking causality, but with finding causes, which,
L201@P4: due to the expressive type of causes, algorithmically boils down to finding executions avoiding the effect
L202@P4: with a minimal distance to the given one.
L203@P4: Based on counterfactuality, Halpern and Pearl [18, 19, 16] provided an influential formalization of
L204@P4: causality using structural equation models, which has served as the basis for various notions of causality
L205@P4: in the verification context (see,e.g., [7, 24]). A key ingredient is the notion of intervention to provide
L206@P4: a semantics for the counterfactual implication in Hume’s definition of causality. An intervention in a
L207@P4: structural equation model sets a variable to a certain value by force, ignoring its dependencies on other
L208@P4: variables, and evaluates the effects of this enforced change. In a sense, a minimal set of interventions
L209@P4: to avoid a cause then leads to a most similar execution avoiding the cause. We will discuss the relations
L210@P4: between our definition and the Halpern-Pearl definition in more detail in Section 3.3. In [7], interventions
L211@P4: are employed to counterexample traces in transition systems by allowing to flip atomic propositions
L212@P4: along a trace. In contrast to our notion of counterfactual causes, this is tailored for complex linear time
L213@P4: properties, but does not provide insights for reachability and safety. Furthermore, the flipping of atomic
L214@P4: propositions can be seen as a change in the transition system while our definition considers alternative
L215@P4: executions without manipulating the system. In [11], the Halpern-Pearl approach is applied to provide
L216@P4: a counterfactual definition of causality in reactive systems. A distance partial order, namely the subset
L217@P4: relation on sets of positions at which traces differ, is used to describe which interventions are acceptable
L218@P4: as they constitute minimal changes necessary to avoid the cause. Checking causality is shown to be
L219@P4: decidable by a formulation as a hyperlogic model-checking problem. Furthermore, notions of necessary
L220@P4: and sufficient causes as sets of states in transition systems have been considered [3]. These do not rely
L221@P4: on the counterfactuality principle and are of forward-looking nature.
L222@P4: We are not aware of formalisations of causality in game structures. The related concept of responsibility, has been investigated in multi-agent models [40, 41]. Notions of forward and backward responsibility of players in multi-player game structures with acyclic tree-like arena have been studied [4].
L223@P4: For a detailed overview of work on causality and related concepts in operational models, we refer the
L224@P4: reader to the survey articles [8, 2].

L276@P5: 3 Counterfactual causes in transition systems
L277@P5: In this section, we introduce the backward-looking notion of counterfactual causes in transition systems
L278@P5: using distance functions (Section 3.1). Afterwards, we prove that the definition can be checked in polynomial time for three well-known distance functions (Section 3.2). Finally, we illustrate similarities
L279@P5: between our notion of counterfactual causality to the definition of causality by Halpern and Pearl (Sec
L280@P5: 3.3). Proofs omitted here can be found in Appendix A.
L281@P5: 3.1 Definition
L282@P5: The effects we consider are reachability or safety properties Φ = ♢E or Φ = 2¬E for a set of states E.
L283@P5: As the behavior of the system after E has been seen is not relevant for these properties, we assume that
L284@P5: E consists of terminal states.
L285@P5: Definition 2 (d-counterfactual cause in transition systems). Let T be a transition system and let d be a
L286@P5: distance function on the set of maximal paths of T . Let E be a set of terminal states and let C be a set of
L287@P5: states disjoint from E. Let Φ = ♢E or Φ = 2¬E. Given a maximal path π that visits C and satisfies Φ
L288@P5: in T , we say that C is a d-counterfactual cause for Φ on π if
L289@P5: 1. there is a maximal path ρ in T that does not visit C, and
L290@P5: 2. all maximal paths ρ with ρ ⊨ 2¬C with minimal distance to π do not satisfy Φ. In other words,

L316@P6: The prefix metric measures similarity in a temporal way saying that executions are more similar if
L317@P6: they initially agree for a longer period of time. If no further structure of the transition system or meaning

L319@P6: Hamming distance dHamm: Given two words w = w0 ...wn and v = v0 ... vn of the same length, we
L320@P6: define dHamm(w, v)
L321@P6: def = |{0 ≤ i ≤ n | wi ̸= vi}|. For two maximal paths π and ρ of the same length in
L322@P6: a transition system T with labeling function L, we define dHamm(π,ρ)
L323@P6: def = dHamm(L(π),L(ρ)). So, the
L324@P6: distance between two paths is the Hamming distance of their traces.
L325@P6: The Hamming distance seems to be a reasonable measure if a system naturally proceeds through
L326@P6: different layers, e.g., if a counter is increased in each step. Then, traces are viewed to be more similar if
L327@P6: they agree on more layers. The temporal order of these layers, however, does not play a role.
